sentences.text: The fossil record consists mainly of isolated teeth and vertebral centra, with only a few associated dentitions and vertebral columns discovered.
A nearly complete skeleton suggests the animal had a stout body, a wide head, and powerful jaws similar to a modern tiger shark.
Teeth feature small, well-separated lateral cusplets connected to the main cusp by enamel on the front face.
The root of these teeth is bilobate and possesses a large, shelf-like protuberance on the inner side that becomes smaller towards the back.
A specimen from Kansas measured approximately 5.15 meters and likely lived to be 22 years old.
The genus was described by Sokolov in 1965.
Stomach contents suggest C. crassidens specialized in hunting large marine turtles, including a 2-meter chelonioid turtle found in Italy.
Evidence indicates C. houghtonorum preyed upon hybodont sharks.
C. crassidens was estimated to be about 1.42 meters long at birth, reached sexual maturity between 12 and 17 years, and lived up to 64 years.
C. crassidens likely preferred offshore waters and had a cosmopolitan distribution, unlike other species such as C. houghtonorum which favored shallow water.
Sharks in the Western Interior Seaway likely coexisted through resource partitioning, such as occupying different water depths or specializing in different prey.
Cretodus likely had a moderate swimming speed, slower than the fast-cruising contemporary shark Cretoxyrhina.
A 2026 study using zinc isotope values suggests Cretodus occupied high trophic positions in the Late Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway.
Cretodus lived during the Late Cretaceous, from approximately 100 to 89 million years ago.
Fossils are found in the Western Interior Seaway of North America, as well as in Late Cretaceous strata of Europe, Africa, and possibly Asia.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Cretodus as the Aptian to Campanian stages, from 121.4 to 72.2 million years ago.
